title: Cowboys' Brian Schottenheimer Slams Play-Calling, Gives Brutal Grade After Ravens Loss
body:
Dallas Cowboys offensive coordinator Brian Schottenheimer did not mince words after the team’s 34‑31 defeat to the Baltimore Ravens in Rio de Janeiro, assigning his own play‑calling a failing grade. The candid self‑assessment, delivered in a post‑game press conference, underscored the frustration that has been mounting around Dallas’s once‑potent offense and hinted at a possible overhaul of the unit’s strategic approach as the season progresses.

Schottenheimer, who has been tasked with revitalizing a Cowboys offense that has struggled to find consistency since the 2023 offseason, labeled his own game plan an “F.” He cited a lack of rhythm in the passing attack, predictable down‑and‑distance choices, and missed opportunities to exploit the Ravens’ defensive mismatches. “We were too predictable, we didn’t adapt, and we left the ball in the hands of a defense that was ready for us,” he said, adding that the team’s inability to sustain drives ultimately cost them the win in the final minutes.

The criticism comes at a time when the Cowboys’ offensive line has been plagued by injuries, and quarterback Dak Prescott has faced intermittent pressure that has forced him into uncomfortable throws. Despite a 31‑point output, the Cowboys amassed only 356 total yards, a stark contrast to the 425 yards the Ravens generated. The disparity was most evident in the red‑zone, where Dallas settled for field goals on three separate trips, while Baltimore converted three of its four trips into touchdowns. Schottenheimer highlighted the missed chances, noting that a more aggressive play‑calling approach—particularly on third‑down and goal‑line situations—could have swung the momentum in Dallas’s favor.

Analysts have long debated the balance between a run‑heavy scheme and a more vertical passing attack in Dallas’s playbook. This week’s loss reignited the conversation, especially after the Ravens’ defensive coordinator, Mike Zirwick, praised his unit’s preparation for the Cowboys’ tendencies. “We knew they liked to roll out on third‑and‑long,” Zirwick said in a post‑game interview. “When you’re predictable, you give the defense a blueprint.” The Cowboys’ reliance on short, high‑percentage passes early in the game allowed the Ravens to stack the box and force Dallas into a one‑dimensional attack, a scenario Schottenheimer admitted he should have anticipated.

The fallout from Schottenheimer’s self‑critique could manifest in several ways. First, the Cowboys may look to diversify their play‑calling by incorporating more play‑action passes and deep shots to keep the defense honest. Second, there is growing speculation that the team might consider a personnel shift, potentially giving more snaps to emerging receivers like CeeDee Lamb and Michael Gallup in an effort to stretch the field. Finally, the coaching staff could lean on veteran quarterback Dak Prescott to take a more active role in audibles, allowing him to adjust protection schemes and target selections on the fly.

Looking ahead, the Cowboys face a pivotal stretch of games that will test whether Schottenheimer’s harsh self‑evaluation translates into tangible adjustments. With a divisional matchup against the New York Giants looming, the pressure to demonstrate a more dynamic offensive identity is mounting. If Dallas can convert the candid criticism into a revamped play‑calling strategy, it may not only salvage the season’s trajectory but also restore confidence among a fan base that has grown increasingly impatient with stagnation. The next few weeks will reveal whether the Cowboys can turn an “F” in play‑calling into a passing grade before the playoffs become a distant dream.
